title: VB4-02185
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Minister (the "appellant"), appeals the July 11, 2014 determination of the Refugee Protection Division (the "RPD").
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Minister (the "appellant"), appeals the July 11, 2014 determination of the Refugee Protection Division (the "RPD"). The claim was heard by the RPD on May 30, 2014 with a decision being rendered on the same day. The RPD found that the appellant is a Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the "Act" or "IRPA").1 XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "respondent"), is a citizen of Guatemala.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(c) of IRPA, the Refugee Appeal Division (the "RAD") sets aside the determination of the RPD and refers the matter to the RPD for redetermination by a different Member of that division.
Counsel for the respondent before the RAD is different than she had at the RPD hearing. The Minister intervened before the RPD but only through documents.
Neither the appellant nor the respondent seeks to present "new" evidence to the RAD pursuant to subsection 110(4) of IRPA.

According to the allegations set out in the respondent's Basis of Claim form (BOC),2 the appellant is a citizen of Guatemala. In 2005, the respondent was approached by some men wearing tattoos and hoodies when she was leaving school. The men told her she was now a part of their "maras ms18". The respondent refused and she was beaten.
Sometime after the attack, the respondent was kidnapped by the Maras and gang raped. Even after this incident, the Maras continually harassed and threatened the respondent and her family.

The respondent, her father, and brother decided to flee to the United States (US). They arrived in the US on XXXX 2005. They left behind the respondent's mother and her two siblings. They lived in the US with an uncle. The respondent's father left for Canada in 2010. The respondent and her brother remained in the US. The respondent was sexually abused by her uncle in the US. The respondent, along with her American-born son, arrived in Canada in XXXX of 2013 where she joined her father and made a claim for refugee protection.
The RPD Member heard the respondent's refugee protection claim on May 30, 2014 and found the respondent to be a Convention refugee on the basis of compelling reasons, IRPA's subsection 108(4).

The Minister's submissions as to the grounds of this appeal can be summarized as follows: Did the RPD err in determining that there are compelling reasons for the claimant not to be returned to Guatemala as per section 108(4) of the Act? Is the appellant's identity established in light of the 'new evidence' before RAD?

The Minister requests3 that the RAD, under paragraph 111(1)(b) of the Act, set aside the determination of the RPD and substitute a determination that, in its opinion, should have been made. The Minister asks that the positive determination of the RPD be set aside and that the RAD substitute a determination that the respondent is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, and pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(c), the Minister requests that the matter be referred back to the RPD for redetermination, giving the directions to the RPD that it considers appropriate.
The respondent requests that the RAD dismiss this appeal and uphold the decision of the RPD Member in this matter.
Although the Act sets out grounds for appeal as well as possible remedies, it does not specify the standard of review to be applied by the RAD.

RAD, being a new division, has struggled with the standard of review to be used in RAD appeals based on several Federal Court cases that have differed in their approach of what standard should be used. Initially, RAD followed the Supreme Court of Canada (the "Supreme Court") case Dunsmuir4 as the leading case on standard of review. In Dunsmuir, the Supreme Court has said that there should be only two standards when reviewing decisions of administrative tribunals: unreasonableness and correctness. The standard of correctness applies to questions of law, while the standard of reasonableness applies to questions of fact, and mixed fact and law.

In recent months, the Federal Court has issued differing decisions on the role of RAD when conducting an appeal of the RPD determination. These decisions include the Federal Court cases Iyamuremye,5 Eng,6 Alvarez,7 Huruglica,8 Njeukam,9 Yetna,10 Wahgmo,11 Alyafi,12 among others.

The Federal Court in Iyamuremye addressed the question of the proper standard of review to be applied by the RAD in reviewing RPD findings and confirmed that the appropriate standard of review for questions of fact and mixed fact and law is reasonableness, and the appropriate standard of review for questions of law is correctness: That said, the Court finds that in assessing the reasonableness of the decision, the RAD should, at the very least, have reviewed the evidence that was presented before the RPD and conducted an independent assessment of all the evidence in order to determine whether the RPD, on the basis of the facts and the conditions of the country in question, had properly considered the evidence and reasonably justified its conclusion.13

In Alvarez, Justice Shore said that "the Court is of the view that the RAD must be able to correct any error of law in a decision of the RPD or any palpable or overriding error in the findings of fact or the application of the law to these facts."14 Furthermore, Justice Shore stated that "[w]hen analyzing a decision of the RPD, the RAD must not merely determine whether it was made in a reasonable manner, but, rather, analyze whether the RPD relied on a wrong principle of law or misassessed the facts to the point of making a palpable and overriding error."15 Justice Shore also said in Alvarez that "the RAD must nonetheless perform its own assessment of all the evidence in order to determine whether the RPD relied on a wrong principle of law or misassessed the facts to the point of making a palpable and overriding error."16

In Huruglica, Justice Phelan found that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness and concluded that the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. "It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection." Justice Phelan also states that, "that notion may well justify deference to a RPD's decision in a circumstance where a witness' credibility is critical or determinative. Where there is no adverse finding of credibility, the policy rationale for deference is not sustainable".17

Justice Phelan also found that the RAD's role should be to determine whether the RPD decision is wrong rather than look at whether it was a reasonable decision. Justice Phelan emphasized that the RAD's mandate is to conduct a fact based review. The RAD, Justice Phelan said "must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment... Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision." Furthermore: In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is a 'palpable and overriding error'.18

The Minister submits19 "the RPD's reasons are not adequate and the evidence does not give rise to reasons which could have been offered in support of the RPD's conclusion. In this appeal, the questions in issue are ones of fact and mixed facts and law. In this case, the appropriate standard of review is one of correctness (Alvarez v. Canada(MCI)2014 FC 702). In this recent Federal Court decision Justice Shore stated "...the RAD must nonetheless perform its own assessment of all of the evidence in order to determine whether the RPD relied on a wrong principle of law or misassessed the facts to the point of making a palpable and overriding error."

Counsel for the respondent submits that: Although appeals to the RAD may not be meant completely as de novo hearings, the RAD, upon review of the legislative language, can consider the substantive merits of the matter including new evidence. AS well, the RAD may make final decisions as to whether or not an individual should have refugee protection.20

The Huruglica decision is the most thorough of all the recent cases and the first one where the Federal Court has certified a question for the Federal Court of Appeal. Again, I refer to paragraphs 54 and 55 of Huruglica which read as follows: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision.21 [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error."22

Following the Huruglica decision, many other cases have followed the Huruglica approach in what the role of the RAD should be in assessing an appeal. There is another line of authority that suggest that the standard that RAD should apply is that of "palpable and overriding error" (Eng23, Alvarez24, Spasoja25). In Alyafi26, Djoussou27, and Siliya28, the Federal Court notes that there are two competing approaches in the Federal Court jurisprudence and that the RAD Member is free to decide which approach to follow.

In Kanga,29 the Federal Court held: Furthermore, even where there is divided Federal Court authority on a point of law, I do not agree that the Board is required to explain why it has adopted one view over the other. Presumably, Federal court jurisprudence speaks for itself and the Board has no obligation to offer any additional interpretation of the legal authorities that it chooses to rely upon in resolving a point of law.

In this particular appeal, however, we are dealing with an error in law in regard to the alleged errors in applying the test for compelling reasons in the RPD determination. It is clear from the many recent Federal Court cases that have been previously mentioned, all agree that the standard of correctness should be used for any error of law found in the RPD decision on appeal to the RAD.

I will now turn to the specific submissions by the appellant as to errors allegedly made by the RPD Member. The error alleged by the appellant regarding the RPD's assessment of compelling reasons is a question of law.
paragraphs.heading_before: ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: The Minister submits that "section 108(4) of the Act permits a decision-maker to grant refugee protection in cases where the applicant has established that they experienced appalling past persecution despite the fact that the original reasons for seeking protection no longer exist." The Minister further submits that: Case law has determined that two conditions must be met before the Board may consider the compelling reasons argument. First the claimant must establish that they would have met the definition of a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. And secondly there must be a determination that the claimant no longer meets either of these definitions because of a change of circumstances. 30

Furthermore, the Minister submits that "the Member did not specifically conduct an analysis about how the claimant meets the definition of Convention refugee. The Member failed to state what link the claim had to any of the Convention grounds therefore a nexus was not established". Finally, the Minister submits that "the past persecution experienced by the claimant does not rise to the level of atrocious or appalling". 31

The respondent submits that "the RPD Board's decision is correct and should be upheld." The respondent submits that the "Member made a finding that the respondent was a Convention refugee based on the nexus of gender". The respondent also submits that: The Respondent's case fits precisely into the parameters of what the compelling reasons doctrine entails, as interpreted by the UNHCR. The Respondent has suffered extreme sexual violence. She was stalked and gang-raped. This is precisely what that compelling reasons exception is meant for.32

It has been established that the compelling reasons exception only applies when there has been a determination that a person would have been a Convention refugee or person in need of protection, but that the conditions that led to such a finding no longer exist.33 In particular, section 10834 of IRPA states the following: 108 (1) A claim for refugee protection shall be rejected, and a person is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, in any of the following circumstances: (e) the reasons for which the person sought refugee protection have ceased to exist.

Subsection 108(4) states that: Paragraph (1)(e) does not apply to a person who establishes that there are compelling reasons arising out of previous persecution, torture, treatment or punishment for refusing to avail themselves of the protection of the country which they left, or outside of which they remained, due to such previous persecution, torture, treatment or punishment.35

In reviewing the RPD Member's decision, I find that the RPD Member did state it is a gender based claim. However, the RPD Member did not go further to explain the gender based claim. In my assessment of the facts, I note that the respondent is a victim of gender based violence and sexual assault. In the Federal Court case, Dezameau,36 the Court found that the error of the Board was to use its finding of a widespread risk of violence in Haitian society to rebut the assertion that there is a nexus between the applicant's social group and the risk of rape. In my evaluation of the evidence, I find the respondent does have a nexus to a Convention Ground. But nexus is just one of the elements of the definition; it is not the end of the analysis.

In the Federal Court case Lici, the Federal Court stated: Before the Board can even consider whether there are sufficient compelling reasons to grant refugee status the claimant must establish that, at some point in time, they would have met the definition of a Convention refugee or person in need of protection. There must also be a determination that they no longer meet these definitions because of a change of circumstances.37

The RPD Member found the respondent was a Convention refugee. The RPD Member finds "I find that you are a Convention refugee - I am basing that on compelling reasons today as I don't believe that you have a forward-looking risk of persecution but I am going to accept you under section 96". In applying sections 96 and 97 of IRPA, the Federal Court has held that the compelling reasons exception only applies when there has been a determination that the person was a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, and also that the conditions that led to that finding no longer exist.38 However, the RPD Member failed to explain how the respondent met the definition of Convention refugee. I find the RPD Member did not conduct a fulsome analysis of all the elements required to conclude that a person is a Convention refugee.

Furthermore, the "compelling reasons" exception arises only when the reasons for which the person sought protection "have ceased to exist". Therefore, there must be a change in circumstances to trigger the consideration of this exception. The RPD Member did refer to the fact that the respondent's 'personal profile has changed'. 39 The RPD Member further states that "I think after this considerable amount of time and the fact that you are no longer similarly situated to yourself as you were as a high school girl, I don't find that your particular profile is linked to the objective evidence before me."40 And: I don't see that you would have a forward-looking risk under section 96 that it would not be more than a mere possibility that you would continue to be targeted by these persons. But counsel has argued that this may be an issue and that the reasons for which you were persecuted have ceased to exist, and that's where section 108 comes into play.41

Although I agree that the respondent's situation may fall into the category of 'changed circumstance', some of the other elements of definition of Convention refugee, such as state protection and internal flight alternative were not considered. How did the RPD Member come to the conclusion that the respondent is a Convention refugee? These are all essential elements that must be analyzed by the RPD Member before considering whether the respondent's past persecution is one of the extraordinary cases in which the persecution is relatively so exceptional, that even in the wake of changed circumstances, it would be wrong to return the refugee claimant to Guatemala. However, the RPD Member failed to properly explain how she found the appellant to be a Convention refugee.

In Cortez,42 the Trial Division held that the applicability of paragraph 2(2)(e) and subsection 2(3) of the Immigration Act,43 now paragraph 108(1)(e) and subsection 108(4) of IRPA was dependent on a finding that the claimant had a well-founded fear of persecution when the person left his or her country of nationality. The reasons for one's fear of persecution have to have ceased thereafter for the compelling reasons exception to be triggered.44 However, the evidentiary burden remains on the claimants to adduce the evidence necessary to establish that they are entitled to the benefit of this provision. It has been established that the compelling reasons exception only applies when there has been a determination that a person would have been a Convention refugee or person in need of protection, but that the conditions that led to such a finding no longer exist.45

In Alharazim,46 the Federal Court noted that: It is settled law that the RPD is entitled to proceed directly to a forward-looking assessment of whether the applicant for refugee protection has a well-founded fear of future persecution, without first making a determination of whether a person has suffered past persecution and, if so, whether subsection 108(4) applies.

The Federal Court went on to say that notwithstanding this, and given the underlying spirit of the provision, "there may be some circumstances in which the nature of past persecution is so severe, that it would be contrary to that spirit and a reviewable error for anyone reviewing an application for refugee protection in such situations to fail to consider the potential applicability of that provision."

Although the RPD Member made errors in her Convention refugee determination as outlined above, I have also assessed whether her ongoing analysis of compelling reasons was correct in law. The RPD Member states in her reasons that there are compelling reasons, there is no persuasive evidence before me as to how the RPD Member came to this conclusion based on the evidence before her. The RPD Member has not provided any analysis on how she came to this conclusion based on the evidence before her. Courts have said that "the Refugee Protection Division is required to assess whether or not the nature of the persecution in a particular case before it constitutes "compelling reasons", and it must explain why the reprehensible treatment, does or does not meet the requirements of section 108(4) of IRPA."47

The issue as to whether "compelling reasons" exist in a given case is a question of fact.48 Each case must be assessed and decided on its own merits, based on the totality of the evidence. However, the delineation of the concept of "compelling reasons" is a question of law.49 In my review, I find the RPD Member has made an error in law by not defining, or providing proper reasons on how the respondent is a Convention refugee. Overall, I find the RPD Member has failed to provide clear reasons as to how the respondent fits into the category of compelling reasons. I find the RPD Member failed to complete her analysis in her determination that the respondent has 'compelling reasons' to be granted refugee protection in Canada.

I considered whether I could substitute the RPD determination by doing an independent assessment of the claim (as directed by Huruglica), but I cannot in the absence of an oral hearing. Subsection 110(3) of the Act requires that the RAD proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the RPD Record, while allowing the RAD to accept documentary evidence and submissions from the Minister and the appellant. According to subsection 110(6), the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in subsection 110(3) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the appellant, that is central to the RPD decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. When read together, subsections 110(3), (4), and (6) establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal such as this unless there is new evidence.50 In this appeal, no new evidence was admitted by either party, and I therefore allow the appeal and refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.

For all these reasons, I set aside the determination of the RPD and refer the claim of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted Panel as per paragraph 111(1) (c) of the IRPA.
